Paper Content:
Preprint
WIDER OR DEEPER?
SCALING LLM INFERENCE-TIME COMPUTE WITH
ADAPTIVE BRANCHING TREE SEARCH
Kou Misaki, Yuichi Inoue, Yuki Imajuku, So Kuroki, Taishi Nakamura, Takuya Akiba
Sakana AI, Japan
{kou.misaki, takiba}@sakana.ai
ABSTRACT
Recent advances demonstrate that increasing inference-time computation can significantly boost the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Although repeated sampling (i.e., generating multiple candidate outputs) is a highly
effective strategy, it does not leverage external feedback signals for refinement,
which are often available in tasks like coding. In this work, we propose Adaptive
Branching Monte Carlo Tree Search (AB-MCTS), a novel inference-time framework that generalizes repeated sampling with principled multi-turn exploration
and exploitation. At each node in the search tree, AB-MCTS dynamically decides whether to “go wider” by expanding new candidate responses or “go deeper”
by revisiting existing ones based on external feedback signals. We evaluate our
method on complex coding and engineering tasks using frontier models. Empirical results show that AB-MCTS consistently outperforms both repeated sampling
and standard MCTS, underscoring the importance of combining the response diversity of LLMs with multi-turn solution refinement for effective inference-time
scaling.

INTRODUCTION
Recent work (Li et al., 2022; Lewkowycz et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025) has
begun to reveal that scaling inference-time computation can significantly boost the performance of
large language models (LLMs) on complex tasks. Traditionally, LLM performance improvements
have stemmed from training-time scaling—namely, increasing the size of training datasets, model
parameters, and computational resources at training (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). In
contrast, inference-time scaling seeks to improve the performance of an LLM by allocating more
computational resources at inference. As we outline in Section 2, there are broadly three types of
approaches to achieve inference-time scaling: post-training tuning, reward-guided CoT (Chain-ofThought), and multiple answer generation. In this paper, we focus on the multiple answer generation
approach, which achieves inference-time scaling by generating multiple candidate answers. This
approach aims to enhance the LLM’s reasoning and problem-solving abilities on-the-fly, without
further training (Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2024; Shinn
et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Antoniades et al.,
2024; Ma et al., 2024). This approach is complementary to other approaches and can easily be
incorporated to achieve even higher performance.
A prominent approach of inference-time scaling is repeated sampling, which encompasses methods
such as best-of-n sampling, majority voting, or self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023; Brown et al.,
2024; Liang et al., 2024). In this approach, multiple candidate outputs are generated independently
from the same prompt, and a final solution is chosen—often via simple heuristics. Repeated sampling has proven effective in challenging tasks such as coding competitions (Li et al., 2022) and the
ARC Challenge (Greenblatt, 2024). This strategy leverages the vast output space of LLMs, allowing us to sample a wide variety of distinct responses from a single prompt. The success of repeated
sampling illustrates that harnessing this capacity is paramount to achieving effective inference-time
scaling.

Figure 1: A visual comparison of the proposed Adaptive Branching MCTS (AB-MCTS) against
three baseline approaches. Repeated sampling generates multiple answers at once (wide but shallow), sequential refinement iteratively revises a single solution (deep but narrow), and standard
MCTS applies a fixed branching factor. In contrast, AB-MCTS dynamically decides whether to
branch out or refine deeper in each iteration, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation.
However, repeated sampling focuses exclusively on exploration and lacks an explicit mechanism
for exploitation. In certain real-world scenarios, one can obtain external feedback on a candidate
solution. For instance, in coding tasks, one can run tests to evaluate the correctness of generated
programs and gather feedback on how to improve them (Madaan et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2024;
Jain et al., 2024). In such settings, it is natural to select promising solutions and refine them based
on available feedback, which repeated sampling alone cannot accomplish effectively. Indeed, prior
studies (Gou et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024) have demonstrated that incorporating external feedback
leads to improvements, underscoring the importance of using such feedback.
Various approaches have been proposed for exploration and exploitation in such multi-turn settings,
but the majority were designed before the power of inference-time scaling was fully recognized.
As a result, they are not scalable, i.e., the gain diminishes when the inference-time computational
budget is increased. This is essentially because these methods use a fixed “width”—that is, they treat
the number of answers generated from the same prompt as a fixed hyperparameter. For example,
methods based on standard Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) use a fixed branching factor (i.e., the
number of child nodes per state) as a hyperparameter (Zhou et al., 2024; Antoniades et al., 2024; Ma
et al., 2024). As demonstrated by the success of repeated sampling, effective inference-time scaling
requires leveraging a vast output space, so a fixed width hinders scaling.
In this work, we propose Adaptive Branching Monte Carlo Tree Search (AB-MCTS), a novel
inference-time framework that generalizes repeated sampling with multi-turn exploration and exploitation (Figure 1). Unlike traditional MCTS or beam search, AB-MCTS does not fix the width
as a static hyperparameter. Instead, at each node of the search tree, AB-MCTS adaptively decides
whether to “go wider” by generating new candidate responses or “go deeper” by refining existing
ones, leveraging external feedback signals. Under the hood, we formalize our decision process
via Bayesian posterior updates, ensuring each expansion balances exploration and exploitation in a
principled manner. This design naturally extends repeated sampling, allowing us to harness the vast
output space of LLMs when necessary. Consequently, our framework provides a powerful mechanism for balancing exploration and exploitation in the context of LLM inference-time scaling.
We evaluated AB-MCTS on complex coding and machine learning engineering benchmarks (Li
et al., 2022; Chan et al., 2024) using frontier models such as GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) and DeepSeek2

V3 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), in a scenario that scales up test-time compute by allowing multiple generation calls for each task instance. Under the same computational budget, AB-MCTS consistently
achieved better results than previous approaches such as repeated sampling and standard MCTS.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• Simultaneous Use of Vast Output Space and Solution Refinement as a New Challenge.
We highlight the vast output space of LLMs as a key for inference-time scaling and propose the new paradigm of combining it with solution refinement to manage the exploration–exploitation trade-off.
• AB-MCTS Algorithm. To address this challenge, we introduce AB-MCTS, which systematically decides whether to “go wide” or “go deep.” We present two variants AB-MCTS-M
and AB-MCTS-A based on different principles, each offering distinct trade-offs.
• Empirical Validation on Frontier Models and Complex Tasks. In a practical setting using
frontier models and real-world complex tasks, we show that AB-MCTS consistently outperforms existing methods.

RELATED WORK
Recent studies have increasingly focused on scaling up the compute budget at inference time to enhance the performance of LLMs. Similar to the scaling laws for training compute budgets (Kaplan
et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), several works have shown that performance benefits can also be
realized by increasing inference-time compute (Li et al., 2022; Lewkowycz et al., 2022; Brown et al.,
2024; Wu et al., 2025). To position our work within the broader research landscape, we review existing approaches to allocating additional computational resources at inference time. Broadly, these
approaches can be grouped into three categories: (1) post-training tuning, (2) reward-guided CoT
(Chain-of-Thought), and (3) multiple answer generation. In the paragraphs that follow, we review
each category and clarify its connection to our proposed method. We also clarify the difference of
our approach from existing MCTS adaptive branching methods.
Inference-Time Scaling by Post-Training Tuning.
A prominent line of research (Jaech et al.,
2024; OpenAI et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Team
et al., 2025) employs post-training strategies that encourage more elaborate reasoning. Representative examples include OpenAI o1 (Jaech et al., 2024), o3 (OpenAI et al., 2025), and DeepSeek-R1
(DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), where reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning using chainof-thought trajectories deepens LLM reasoning. These techniques enhance the LLM’s ability to
produce a single answer more effectively. In contrast, we focus on a framework that repeatedly uses
the LLM to generate multiple candidate answers, carrying out trial-and-error with external feedback.
Consequently, these lines of research are orthogonal to ours.
Inference-Time Scaling via Reward-Guided CoT.
Another approach to scaling up test-time
computation—particularly in mathematical tasks—is to incrementally generate each reasoning step
(Lewkowycz et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). Here, a trained reward model often guides the
validity of each step, where each step corresponds to a single sentence within an answer (Hao et al.,
2023; Yao et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2024; Qi
et al., 2024; Guan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). While this demonstrates the
value of inference-time scaling, it typically relies on internal (model-based) reward estimates rather
than utilizing external feedback. Moreover, even in MCTS-based works for step-by-step reasoning,
the branching factor is fixed (Hao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024;
Park et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025), thereby failing to leverage the vast output space of LLMs. Furthermore, since this approach focuses on enhancing the performance of generating a single answer
without external feedback, it is orthogonal to our research.
Inference-Time Scaling by Multiple Answer Generation.
The approaches closely related to
ours involve generating multiple candidate answers at inference time and then selecting or refining
them. This approach is in contrast to the reward-guided CoT approach, where each LLM output corresponds to a single reasoning step, rather than a full answer. Early work adopted a self-consistency
strategy, in which the model produces several answers and the best is chosen (Li et al., 2022; Wang

et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2024). While straightforward, this approach does not refine answers in
response to external signals. To improve beyond simple selection, some studies have introduced
mechanisms for mutating or refining candidate answers (Madaan et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2024),
naturally suggesting a tree-based search formulation. For example, tree expansions driven by LLMs
(Li et al., 2024) or Bayesian methods (Tang et al., 2024) have been explored, although these works
do not employ MCTS. Lee et al. (2025) proposes an evolutionary method for answer refinement
but relies on crossover operations, which are not always straightforward to define. When MCTS
is employed for answer exploration, it typically relies on a fixed number of children per node. For
instance, Zhou et al. (2024) introduce Language Agent Tree Search (LATS), which unifies reasoning, acting, and planning in large language models by integrating MCTS with LM-powered value
functions and self-reflection. In the software engineering domain, Antoniades et al. (2024) propose
SWE-Search, a multi-agent framework that enhances software agents via MCTS and iterative selfimprovement, enabling agents to refine their strategies over multiple solution attempts. Similarly,
Ma et al. (2024) present RepoUnderstander, where LLM-based agents build a repository knowledge
graph in a top-down manner, employ MCTS to explore the repository, and then leverage structured information to generate patches for real-world GitHub issues. Although each approach differs
mainly in the design of rewards and actions, they generally adopt “standard MCTS”, by which we
mean the conventional MCTS method with a fixed number of child nodes. These methods integrate
MCTS into LLM-based decision-making without proposing a new search algorithm from scratch.
We refer to these conventional MCTS strategies collectively as “standard MCTS” and compare them
with our proposed framework in subsequent sections.
Adaptive Node Branching in MCTS.
Although prior work has explored adaptive branching
strategies in MCTS—for instance, progressive widening (Coulom, 2007) and double progressive
widening (Couëtoux et al., 2011)—these methods typically rely on heuristic branching rules derived
from visitation counts. In contrast, our AB-MCTS method adaptively branches off by leveraging
external feedback rather than simply tracking node visits. Also, while these methods focus on
the number of children per node, our AB-MCTS method does not fix the width as a static hyperparameter.
Instead, at each node of the search tree, AB-MCTS adaptively decides whether to “go wider” by
generating new candidate responses or “go deeper” by revisiting existing ones, leveraging external feedback signals. Under the hood, we formalize our decision process via Bayesian posterior updates, ensuring each expansion balances exploration and exploitation in a principled manner. This design naturally extends repeated
sampling, allowing us to harness the vast output space of LLMs when necessary. Consequently, our
framework provides a powerful mechanism for balancing exploration and exploitation in the context of
LLM inference-time scaling. We evaluated AB-MCTS on complex coding and machine learning engineering benchmarks (Li et al., 2022; Chan et al., 2024) using frontier models such as GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) and
DeepSeek2 V3 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), in a scenario that scales up test-time compute by allowing multiple
generation calls for each task instance. Under the same computational budget, AB-MCTS consistently
achieved better results than previous approaches such as repeated sampling and standard MCTS.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• Simultaneous Use of Vast Output Space and Solution Refinement as a New Challenge.
We highlight the vast output space of LLMs as a key for inference-time scaling and propose the new
paradigm of combining it with solution refinement to manage the exploration–exploitation trade-off.
• AB-MCTS Algorithm. To address this challenge, we introduce AB-MCTS, which systematically decides whether to “go wide” or “go deep.” We present two variants AB-MCTS-M and AB-MCTS-A based on different principles, each offering distinct trade-offs.
• Empirical Validation on Frontier Models and Complex Tasks. In a practical setting using frontier
models and real-world complex tasks, we show that AB-MCTS consistently outperforms existing methods.

INTRODUCTION
In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various
fields, but their inference time often limits their application in real-world scenarios. To address this
problem, researchers have explored various approaches to scale up the compute budget at inference time.
One promising direction is to leverage the vast output space of LLMs, allowing multiple candidate
answers to be generated and refined.
